subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Reference frames and what makes one inertial
Galilean relativity: the same mechanics in every inertial frame
The two postulates of special relativity
The Lorentz transformation and the Lorentz factor
The space–time interval is the same for every observer
The slope of a world line gives the speed
Muon decay as evidence for time dilation and length contraction

questions.q: Treat the Earth's surface as an inertial reference frame. Which of the following is also an inertial reference frame?
options: A car going round a circular roundabout at a steady 30 m s⁻¹
A lift at the instant it is at rest while reversing direction
A rocket whose engine gives it a uniform acceleration of 3 m s⁻²
A train on a straight, level track at a steady 30 m s⁻¹
optionWhy: A student who equates constant speed with constant velocity picks this. The car's direction is changing, so it has a centripetal acceleration and its frame is not inertial.
A student who thinks zero velocity means zero acceleration picks this. The lift's velocity is changing through zero, so it is accelerating at that instant and its frame is not inertial.
A student who reads 'uniform' as 'steady motion' picks this. A uniform acceleration is still an acceleration, and an inertial frame must be non-accelerating.

The train's velocity (speed and direction) is constant, so it is not accelerating. A non-accelerating frame is an inertial frame: in it a ball placed on a table stays at rest, just as it would on the ground.
questions.explain: The train's velocity (speed and direction) is constant, so it is not accelerating. A non-accelerating frame is an inertial frame: in it a ball placed on a table stays at rest, just as it would on the ground.
questions.working: Inertial frame = non-accelerating. Train: straight track, constant speed → constant velocity, a = 0. Roundabout: direction changes, a = v²/r ≠ 0. Reversing lift: v = 0 momentarily but Δv/Δt ≠ 0. Rocket: a = 3 m s⁻² ≠ 0.

questions.q: A passenger in a train moving along a straight track at constant velocity drops a ball from rest relative to the train. Where does the ball land, and why?
options: Behind the point of release, as the floor moves on while the ball is falling.
Directly below the point of release, as the air in the carriage carries it.
Directly below the point of release, as it keeps the train's horizontal velocity.
Directly below the point of release, and it falls vertically for the platform.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a released object is 'left behind' picks this. The ball already has the train's horizontal velocity and nothing changes it, so it keeps pace with the floor.

A student who credits the moving air with keeping objects up with the train picks this. The ball keeps the train's velocity by Newton's first law. The carriage air moves with the train and exerts no horizontal push; the result is the same in a vacuum.

Before release the ball moves with the train. No horizontal force acts after release, so it keeps that horizontal velocity and stays level with the release point. Galilean relativity: the result is the same as in a stationary train.

A student who thinks the ball's motion is the same in every frame picks this. On the platform the ball has the train's horizontal velocity as it falls, so it follows a curved (parabolic) path, not a vertical line.
questions.explain: Before release the ball moves with the train. No horizontal force acts after release, so it keeps that horizontal velocity and stays level with the release point. Galilean relativity: the result is the same as in a stationary train.
questions.working: Train frame: horizontal velocity 0, falls vertically, lands below release point. Platform frame: horizontal velocity = train's velocity, parabolic path; lands at the point that is then below the release point.

questions.q: In Galilean relativity the time of an event in frame S′ is related to its time in frame S by t′ = t. What does this equation state?
options: Both observers give each event the same time, whatever their relative motion.
Each observer gives a later time to an event the further away from them it happens.
The moving observer's clock runs slow, so it gives a smaller time to each event.
Only the observer at rest gives the true time; the moving one must correct it.
optionWhy: t′ = t is the Galilean assumption that time is absolute: all inertial observers assign the same time to every event, so they agree on time intervals and on simultaneity.
A student who dates an event by when its light arrives picks this. The time of an event is read on a clock at the event; t′ = t says the two frames' clocks agree for every event, wherever it is.
A student who carries time dilation into Galilean relativity picks this. Galilean relativity has no time dilation: t′ = t exactly. Slow-running clocks belong to special relativity.
A student who thinks one frame is really at rest picks this. t′ = t says both observers give the same time, so there is nothing to correct and neither frame is preferred.
questions.explain: t′ = t is the Galilean assumption that time is absolute: all inertial observers assign the same time to every event, so they agree on time intervals and on simultaneity.
questions.working: t′ = t for all events → identical time coordinates, intervals and simultaneity in every inertial frame (absolute time).

questions.q: On a straight road, car A travels east at 35 m s⁻¹ and car B travels west at 22 m s⁻¹, both relative to the road. Take east as the positive direction. What is the velocity of car B in the reference frame of car A?
options: +57 m s⁻¹
−57 m s⁻¹
−13 m s⁻¹
−22 m s⁻¹
optionWhy: A student who calculates v − u = 35 − (−22) = +57 m s⁻¹ has found the velocity of A in B's frame. The velocity of B relative to A is u − v, which is negative.
In A's frame, v = +35 m s⁻¹ and B's velocity in the road frame is u = −22 m s⁻¹. u′ = u − v = −22 − 35 = −57 m s⁻¹: B approaches A at 57 m s⁻¹, moving west.
A student who ignores directions and subtracts the speeds gets 22 − 35 = −13 m s⁻¹. B moves west, so u = −22 m s⁻¹, and the magnitudes combine.
A student who thinks B's velocity is the same for every observer gives its road-frame value. In A's frame the relative velocity of the frames must be subtracted: u′ = u − v.
questions.explain: In A's frame, v = +35 m s⁻¹ and B's velocity in the road frame is u = −22 m s⁻¹. u′ = u − v = −22 − 35 = −57 m s⁻¹: B approaches A at 57 m s⁻¹, moving west.
questions.working: u = −22 m s⁻¹ (B, road frame), v = +35 m s⁻¹ (A relative to road). u′ = u − v = −22 − 35 = −57 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A spacecraft travels directly towards a distant star at 0.60c relative to the star. An astronaut measures the speed of the starlight arriving at the spacecraft. What does the astronaut find?
options: 1.6c, as the speed of the spacecraft towards the star adds to the speed of light
c, but only as the star is at rest; light from a moving star would be faster
0.40c, as the spacecraft's speed is subtracted from the speed of light
c, as the speed of light in a vacuum does not depend on the motion of the observer
optionWhy: A student who applies Galilean velocity addition to light adds the speeds. Experiment shows light has speed c for all inertial observers, so u′ = u − v does not apply to light.
A student who thinks a moving source changes the speed of light picks this. The second postulate states that c is independent of the motion of the source as well as of the observer.

A student who finds a relative speed by subtracting the smaller speed from the larger, ignoring that the spacecraft and the light are moving towards each other, gets c − 0.60c = 0.40c. By the second postulate the speed of light in a vacuum is c for all inertial observers, so the astronaut measures c.

By the second postulate every inertial observer measures the speed of light in a vacuum to be c, whatever the motion of source or observer. The spacecraft's speed changes the light's frequency and wavelength, not its speed.
questions.explain: By the second postulate every inertial observer measures the speed of light in a vacuum to be c, whatever the motion of source or observer. The spacecraft's speed changes the light's frequency and wavelength, not its speed.
questions.working: Second postulate: the speed of light in a vacuum = c for all inertial observers. Neither Galilean addition (c + 0.60c = 1.6c) nor subtraction of speeds (c − 0.60c = 0.40c) applies; the astronaut measures c.

questions.q: Frame S′ moves at v = 0.80c in the positive x-direction relative to frame S, and the origins coincide at t = t′ = 0. An event occurs at x = 900 m, t = 1.0 μs in S. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the position x′ of the event in S′?
optionWhy: A student who leaves out γ calculates x − vt = 900 − 240 = 660 m, which is the Galilean value. At 0.80c, γ = 1.67 multiplies the bracket.
A student who divides by γ calculates 660/1.67 = 396 m. The Lorentz transformation multiplies (x − vt) by γ.
A student who adds vt calculates 1.67 × (900 + 240) = 1900 m. The origin of S′ has moved 240 m towards the event, so vt is subtracted.

questions.q: Which statement about the Lorentz factor γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) is correct?
options: It is never greater than 1, and it decreases towards zero as v approaches c.
It increases in direct proportion to v, so it equals 2 when v is half of c.
It is larger for a frame approaching the observer than for one moving away at the same speed.
It is never less than 1, and it increases without limit as v approaches c.
optionWhy: A student who takes γ to be √(1 − v²/c²) itself, rather than its reciprocal, picks this. √(1 − v²/c²) is at most 1, so its reciprocal γ is at least 1.
A student who assumes a linear relationship picks this. At 0.50c, γ = 1/√0.75 = 1.15; γ reaches 2 only at v = 0.87c.
A student who expects γ to behave like the Doppler shift picks this. γ depends on v², so approach and recession at the same speed give the same γ.
γ = 1 at v = 0, is greater than 1 for any non-zero v, and 1 − v²/c² tends to zero as v approaches c, so γ grows without limit. It has the same value for either direction of motion.
questions.explain: γ = 1 at v = 0, is greater than 1 for any non-zero v, and 1 − v²/c² tends to zero as v approaches c, so γ grows without limit. It has the same value for either direction of motion.
questions.working: γ(0) = 1; γ(0.50c) = 1/√0.75 = 1.15; γ(0.87c) ≈ 2.0; γ → ∞ as v → c. Depends on v², so direction does not matter.

questions.q: In the Earth's frame S, spacecraft A moves at +0.60c and spacecraft B moves at −0.50c along the same line, towards each other. Frame S′ is the rest frame of A. Using u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²), what is the velocity of B in S′?
optionWhy: A student who uses Galilean addition, u − v = −0.50c − 0.60c, gets −1.10c. That exceeds c; the relativistic denominator 1 − uv/c² = 1.30 is needed.
A student who drops the signs in the denominator uses 1 − 0.30 = 0.70 and gets −1.10c/0.70 = −1.57c. uv = (−0.50c)(0.60c) is negative, so the denominator is 1 + 0.30 = 1.30.
A student who treats B's velocity as +0.50c (ignoring its direction) gets (0.50 − 0.60)/(1 − 0.30) = −0.14c. B moves in the negative direction, so u = −0.50c.

questions.q: Two inertial observers in relative motion measure the same two events. Which quantity do they necessarily agree on?
options: The time interval Δt between the events, as time passes at an equal rate for every observer
The quantity (cΔt)² − (Δx)², the square of the space–time interval between the events
The distance Δx between the two events, as distances do not depend on the frame
The quantity (cΔt)² + (Δx)², the square of the straight-line distance on a space–time diagram
optionWhy: A student who assumes absolute time picks this. In special relativity Δt depends on the frame (for example time dilation); only the combination (cΔt)² − (Δx)² is invariant.
The space–time interval is invariant: every inertial observer calculates the same (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)², even though they measure different Δt and Δx.
A student who thinks distances are the same in every frame picks this. Δx differs between frames even in Galilean relativity when the events are not simultaneous.
A student who applies Pythagoras' theorem to space–time picks this. The invariant has a minus sign: (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)².
questions.explain: The space–time interval is invariant: every inertial observer calculates the same (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)², even though they measure different Δt and Δx.
questions.working: Invariant: (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)². Δt and Δx individually depend on the frame.

questions.q: A muon is created in the upper atmosphere and later decays, moving at 0.99c relative to the Earth throughout. Which observer measures the proper time interval between its creation and its decay?
options: An observer moving with the muon, as both events occur at the same place in that frame
An observer at rest on the Earth, as the Earth is the frame that is not moving
Any observer with an accurate clock, as proper time means the correct time
An observer midway between the events, as light from each reaches them equally fast
optionWhy: The proper time interval is measured in the frame in which the two events occur at the same place. In the muon's rest frame it is created and decays at the same point, so a single clock there measures Δt₀.
A student who treats the Earth as truly at rest picks this. In the Earth frame the creation and decay happen kilometres apart, so the Earth measures a dilated interval, not the proper time.
A student who reads 'proper' as 'correct' picks this. Every inertial observer's measurement is correct for their frame; the proper time is the one measured where both events happen at the same place.

A student who thinks event times depend on when light arrives picks this. Signal delay is always corrected for; the proper time is defined by the two events being at the same place, not by the observer's position.
questions.explain: The proper time interval is measured in the frame in which the two events occur at the same place. In the muon's rest frame it is created and decays at the same point, so a single clock there measures Δt₀.
questions.working: Proper time: frame in which both events occur at the same place → muon rest frame.

questions.q: A spacecraft passes the Earth at 0.80c. A lamp on the spacecraft flashes once every 6.00 min, measured by a clock on the spacecraft. Earth observers time the flashes using clocks at rest in the Earth's frame. What time interval between flashes do they measure?
options: 3.60 min
10.0 min
16.7 min
13.4 min
optionWhy: A student who thinks the Earth measures the shorter interval divides by γ: 6.00/1.667 = 3.60 min. The proper time, measured on the spacecraft, is the shortest interval; the Earth measures γΔt₀.
The spacecraft's clock is present at every flash, so 6.00 min is the proper time Δt₀. γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1.667, so Δt = γΔt₀ = 1.667 × 6.00 = 10.0 min.
A student who omits the square root uses γ = 1/(1 − 0.64) = 2.78, giving 16.7 min. γ = 1/√0.36 = 1.667.
A student who does not square v/c uses γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80) = 2.24, giving 13.4 min. v²/c² = 0.64, so γ = 1.667.
questions.explain: The spacecraft's clock is present at every flash, so 6.00 min is the proper time Δt₀. γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1.667, so Δt = γΔt₀ = 1.667 × 6.00 = 10.0 min.
questions.working: Δt₀ = 6.00 min (spacecraft clock at both flashes). γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1/√0.36 = 1.667. Δt = γΔt₀ = 1.667 × 6.00 min = 10.0 min.

questions.q: A spacecraft has a proper length of 60.0 m. It moves past a space station at 0.60c along its length. What length does an observer on the space station measure for the spacecraft?
optionWhy: A student who multiplies by γ, as in time dilation, gets 60.0 × 1.25 = 75 m. A moving object is measured shorter: L = L₀/γ.
A student who omits the square root in γ uses 1/(1 − 0.36) = 1.5625 and gets 38 m. γ = 1/√0.64 = 1.25.
A student who thinks contraction is only an optical appearance gives the proper length. The station observer really measures L = L₀/γ = 48 m.
γ = 1/√(1 − 0.60²) = 1.25. L = L₀/γ = 60 m/1.25 = 48 m. The spacecraft is shorter along its direction of motion.
questions.explain: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.60²) = 1.25. L = L₀/γ = 60 m/1.25 = 48 m. The spacecraft is shorter along its direction of motion.

questions.q: A lamp at the exact centre of a railway carriage flashes once. The carriage moves at constant high speed past a platform. In the carriage frame, the light reaches the front and rear doors at the same time. According to an observer on the platform, what happens?
options: The light reaches the rear door first, as the rear door moves towards the light.
Both at once, as light going forwards moves at c + v and backwards at c − v.
Both at once, as events simultaneous in one frame are simultaneous in every frame.
The light arrives at both doors together; she only sees one first because it is nearer to her.
optionWhy: In the platform frame both pulses travel at c (second postulate). The rear door moves towards its pulse and the front door away from its pulse, so the rear door is reached first. Events simultaneous in the carriage frame are not simultaneous in the platform frame.
A student who applies Galilean velocity addition to light picks this. In the platform frame both pulses travel at c, so the rear door, moving towards its pulse, is reached first.

A student who assumes absolute simultaneity picks this. Simultaneity is relative: events at different places that are simultaneous in one frame are not simultaneous in a frame moving along the line joining them.
A student who thinks the disagreement is a light-delay effect picks this. Even after correcting for light travel time to the observer, the platform frame assigns the rear-door event the earlier time.
questions.explain: In the platform frame both pulses travel at c (second postulate). The rear door moves towards its pulse and the front door away from its pulse, so the rear door is reached first. Events simultaneous in the carriage frame are not simultaneous in the platform frame.
questions.working: Platform frame: both pulses at c; rear door approaches its pulse, front door recedes from its pulse → rear door reached first.

questions.q: A space–time diagram for frame S has x on the horizontal axis and ct on the vertical axis, with equal scales. Which describes the world lines of a particle at rest in S and of a light pulse?
options: Particle: a single point on the x axis of the diagram. Light pulse: a line at 45° to both axes.
Particle: a line parallel to the x axis. Light pulse: a line at 45° to both axes.
Particle: a line parallel to the ct axis. Light pulse: a line at 45° to both axes.
Particle: a line parallel to the ct axis. Light pulse: a line along the x axis.
optionWhy: A student who reads the diagram as a picture of the path in space picks this. The particle exists at every instant, so it has an event at every ct: a vertical line, not a point.
A student who reads the diagram like a distance–time graph picks this. Here time (ct) is vertical, so a horizontal line joins events at one instant; a particle at rest has a vertical world line.
A particle at rest keeps the same x as ct increases, so its world line is vertical. Light travels a distance cΔt in time Δt, so Δx = Δ(ct) and its world line is at 45°.
A student who treats light as instantaneous picks this. With ct on the time axis, light moves one unit of x for each unit of ct, so its world line is at 45°, not horizontal.
questions.explain: A particle at rest keeps the same x as ct increases, so its world line is vertical. Light travels a distance cΔt in time Δt, so Δx = Δ(ct) and its world line is at 45°.
questions.working: At rest: x constant → line parallel to ct axis. Light: Δx = cΔt = Δ(ct) → 45°.

questions.q: On a space–time diagram with axes x and ct, the world line of a particle moving at constant velocity makes an angle of 25° with the ct axis. What is the speed of the particle?
optionWhy: A student who uses sin θ gets sin 25° = 0.42. The world line moves Δx for each Δ(ct), which is opposite over adjacent: tan θ = v/c.
tan θ = v/c, with θ measured from the ct axis. v = c tan 25° = 0.466c ≈ 0.47c.
A student who measures the angle from the x axis uses tan 65° = 2.14 and gets a speed greater than c. θ is measured from the ct axis: v = c tan 25°.
A student who assumes speed is proportional to angle, with light at 45°, calculates (25/45)c = 0.56c. tan θ is not proportional to θ: v = c tan 25° = 0.47c.
questions.explain: tan θ = v/c, with θ measured from the ct axis. v = c tan 25° = 0.466c ≈ 0.47c.
questions.working: v = c tan θ = c tan 25° = 0.466c ≈ 0.47c.

questions.q: Muons are produced 4.5 km above the ground (measured in the Earth's frame) and travel straight down at 0.995c. What is the thickness of this 4.5 km layer of atmosphere in the muons' rest frame?
optionWhy: A student who multiplies by γ gets 4500 × 10.0 = 45 km. A moving length is contracted: L = L₀/γ.
A student who thinks only the muon, as the 'moving' object, is affected gives the Earth-frame value. In the muons' frame the atmosphere is moving, so it is contracted.
A student who omits the square root uses γ = 1/(1 − 0.995²) = 100 and gets 45 m. γ = 1/√0.009975 = 10.0.
In the muons' frame the atmosphere moves at 0.995c, so it is contracted. γ = 1/√(1 − 0.995²) = 10.0. L = L₀/γ = 4500 m/10.0 = 450 m.
questions.explain: In the muons' frame the atmosphere moves at 0.995c, so it is contracted. γ = 1/√(1 − 0.995²) = 10.0. L = L₀/γ = 4500 m/10.0 = 450 m.
questions.working: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.995²) = 1/√0.009975 = 10.0. Proper length (Earth frame) L₀ = 4500 m. Muon frame: L = L₀/γ = 4500 m/10.0 = 449 m ≈ 4.5 × 10² m.
